newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey stocks ease slightly after Moody's rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Turkey stocks ease slightly after Moody's rate cut.

text.p: Turkish stocks fell slightly on Friday in reaction to a downgrading of Turkey's foreign currency sovereign rating as money markets shrugged off the news which had been discounted by many players, bankers said.

Bankers and brokers said markets remained calm over the rating cut which came after the Islamist-led government agreed at a cabinet meeting on Thursday to implement measures to combat Islamist activism demanded by the secularist military.
Moody's downgraded the long-term foreign currency soverign rating of Turkey to B1 from Ba3 because of a weak fiscal position and political uncertainties.

The IMKB National-100 fell seven points or 0.47 percent in the first session from Thursday's close of 1,504. It had jumped 4.66 percent on Thursday on late buying fuelled by positive expectations sparked by the outcome of the cabinet meeting.

"Some slight selling came today. But the bad and good news came at the same time and the market reacted more to political developments rather than the downgrading," said broker Huseyin Istanbullu from Meksa Securities.

Political tension had mounted early last week due to a row between the Islamists and the army following a February 28 National Security Council (MGK) statement urging action against rising Islamist zeal.

In the currency market, the lira opened weaker at 125,350 to the dollar from 124,730 on Thursday, in line with the dollar's rise in the world markets, but firmed to 125,250 at midday again on parity movements.
Bond yields fell around 1-1.5 points amid liquidity and positive mood created by the cabinet meeting.

"We were awaiting the downgrading for some time, so it was not a surprise for the markets. The news came after the cabinet decisions and trading closed. That also helped markets shrug off the rate cut news," said Ali Ozenc, money market manager at private Finansbank.
He added that political news had more impact on the markets as the cabinet decisions eased political tension and uncertainty over the future of the coalition government at least for some time.

Soner Dolanay, treasurer of the Westdeutsche Landesbank, said Moody's move ended expectations for a downgrading of Turkey's rating. "From now on, there will be no expected rate cuts and the markets will watch political developments."
"Politics will dominate markets and markets are seen in a positive mood in the short term," he told Reuters.
Earlier this month, Duff & Phelps credit rating agency had downgraded rating of the currency obligations to BB minus from BB.
Turkish state minister Sabri Tekir, responsible for state banks, accused rating agencies of failing to carry out "necessary investigations" about the economy.
"Downgrading of Turkey's credit rating will not affect the Turkish economy negatively," Tekir told Reuters.
